runs.t: S1. The directory inventory and its coverage

text: S1. The directory inventory and its coverage

runs.t: The Colorado State Business Directory was published annually from 1871; the Denver Public Library has scanned 34 editions between 1871 and 1956 (1871, 1875, 1877–85, 1887–88, 1891–92, 1910–17, 1920, 1927, 1929, 1932–33, 1935, 1939, 1941, 1943, 1950, 1956). Every listing in the hazardous trades (smelting and refining, foundries, iron and steel and metal working, machine shops, chemicals and paints, petroleum and asphalt, tanneries, rendering and soap, gas works, plating, printing, plastics and rubber) was extracted by optical character recognition and keyword rules, checked by hand for Denver, and geocoded against a street grid built from the historical address ranges; listings with no usable street address are placed at the town centre and are excluded from all spatial analyses.

runs.t: The Directory of Colorado Manufacturers (Business Research Division, University of Colorado, 1961–2002) was scanned from library copies in 25 editions. Twelve of the scans stop part-way through the geographic section or have missing pages (1961, 1962, 1971, 1976, 1979, 1982, 1984, 1985, 1986, 1993, 1999, 2002) and are excluded everywhere; the thirteen complete editions are 1965, 1966, 1967, 1968, 1970, 1973, 1974, 1977, 1980, 1983, 1988, 1990 and 1992. Listings were linked across editions when within 30 m of each other, giving one site per address with first and last years of listing: the 44,808 listings of the complete editions yield 3,487 street-located sites in the hazardous sectors, 1,112 of them in the City and County of Denver (all 25 editions together hold 72,317 listings and 4,669 hazardous-sector sites; that inventory is kept for reference and is not used in the paper). One definition of hazardous industry, the Frickel and Elliott sector set, is used for every count in the paper and the application. Denver's street grid numbers north and south from Ellsworth Avenue and east and west from Broadway. In an earlier build, 34 Denver listings, 25 of them in the 1965 edition, had been placed by the geocoder's direction-loose pass on the unprefixed north-Denver street of a south-Denver address; the geocoder now never places a prefixed address on the unprefixed street across those baselines, and a final check, which sets to unlocated any Denver listing whose point lies on the wrong side of the baseline for the direction in its own address, finds none. Table S1 compares each edition with County Business Patterns.

runs.t: Across 15 editions and 63 counties the log directory count correlates with the log CBP count at r = 0.84 (all manufacturing) and 0.88 (hazardous sectors); Denver's directory/CBP ratio is 0.94. CBP counts every employer establishment from administrative records and the directory lists firms that answered the publisher's questionnaire or were copied from other lists, so the ratios are coverage rates; ratios above 1 (1977, 1980, 1983) mean the directory listed more hazardous-sector firms than CBP counted employer establishments, plausibly because it includes some firms without employees. County files are from Eckert et al. (2021).

S2. Reconstruction of enumeration districts, 1880–1940

runs.t: The IPUMS complete-count files give every person's enumeration district number but no address, and no public source maps the districts of 1900–1940. Brown University's Geographic Reference Files for Denver link household heads in each census to street addresses; these were geocoded with an offline geocoder against the historical street grid, and each district's polygon was drawn as the dissolved Voronoi cells of its geocoded addresses, clipped to the city. Only the districts of Denver itself are used: Arapahoe County's districts before the 1902 consolidation, and the City and County of Denver's from 1910; because district numbers repeat across counties, districts are selected by county as well as number, and the mapped population is checked against the county total (1920: 257,317 of 258,017; 1930: 284,823 of 287,832; 1940: 317,663 of 322,780). Stray geocodes — farther from the district's person-weighted median centre than the larger of 400 m and 2.5 times the median distance, or with fewer than 30% of their ten nearest neighbours in the same district — are dropped before the tessellation, and districts with fewer than three geocoded households were merged with their neighbours. 72% of the 1900 addresses are geocoded at street level, and the addresses kept after stray geocodes are dropped hold 60% of the 1900 population (73% in 1940). For 1880, Brown's Urban Transition Historical GIS geocoded the census to buildings; the districts were rebuilt from those buildings by the same procedure so that all six censuses are constructed alike. The composition measures are population-weighted aggregates of the full count (race, Hispanic origin, nativity, year of immigration, occupation and Duncan socioeconomic index, tenure, rent, household relationship); only aggregates leave the project.

runs.t: A measure is set to missing in a census whose questionnaire or extract does not carry it (ownership in 1880; SEI in the 1900 extract; rent and residence in 1935 except in 1940; 1940 sample-line items), rather than to zero. Hispanic origin is IPUMS HISPAN, inferred from birthplace, parents' birthplace and Spanish surname. "Boarders and lodgers" are household members unrelated to the head (RELATE 12–13). Because the number and size of districts change between censuses, Black–nonblack dissimilarity is also computed on a fixed 500 m grid: each census's district counts are area-weighted onto the grid, using the area mapped in all six censuses (53 cells) and the area mapped from 1900 (310 cells).

runs.t: S3. The 1925 zoning ordinance: classification and georeferencing

text: S3. The 1925 zoning ordinance: classification and georeferencing

runs.t: The Building Zone Map of February 1925 as revised to January 1929 (Denver Public Library, CG4314 .D4 G44 1929) is a monochrome print in which the thirteen districts are drawn as hatch patterns: Residence A blank, Residence B thin diagonal lines, Residence C cross-hatch, Residence D dots, Residence E thick diagonal lines, Business A–C solid black with a letter, Commercial A–C dense cross-hatch with a letter, Industrial A thick diagonal lines rising to the right, Industrial B thick diagonal lines falling to the right. The 11,849 × 12,000-pixel scan was thresholded, and for each pixel the fraction of dark pixels along short line segments in the four orientations was computed; averaging these over 32-pixel cells gives the density of rising-diagonal, falling-diagonal and horizontal/vertical ink and of isolated blobs. Cells were labelled Industrial where one diagonal orientation dominated and there were no horizontal/vertical lot lines (the industrial districts are drawn without block subdivision), Industrial B where the falling diagonal dominated, and Commercial where both diagonals were dense; a second rule labelled thick rising-diagonal hatch with lot lines as Industrial A, which cannot be told from Residence E and is flagged as uncertain (43% of industrial cells). After morphological cleaning and removal of components smaller than ten cells, the map yields 24.8 km² Industrial A, 3.8 km² Industrial B and 3.6 km² Commercial on the whole sheet (the main text's 28.4 km² is the industrial land on the part of the sheet that the 1944 map also covers, within Denver County; its 24.7 km² of Industrial A is the part covered by the 2023 zoning layer).

runs.t: Georeferencing used sixteen street intersections and park corners read off the scan and resolved to TIGER/Line road intersections. One of them, the City Park south-west corner at E 17th Avenue and York Street, was dropped as mis-identified (TIGER's 17th Avenue jogs half a block there); the remaining fifteen all resolve, and an affine fit in UTM zone 13N has a root-mean-square residual of 19 m (individual residuals 1–31 m, the largest at E Colfax Ave and Lincoln St; Table S3). The 1944 revision of the same map (CG4314 .G44 1944, revised to 1 April 1944) was registered to the 1929 scan by a ten-point affine fit (RMSE 25 scan pixels, about 32 m). It is a darker print of the same plate. One texture classifier trained on the 1929 labels was applied to both scans; every cluster of disagreement of about a city block or more (118 of 226 clusters) was inspected on side-by-side crops of the two scans, and only districts visibly redrawn were accepted (8 areas). No industrial district was added between the two revisions; about 0.48 km² of Industrial A (2% of it) was redrawn as commercial, business or apartment districts. Most disagreements came from the darker 1944 print rather than from redrawn districts; changes smaller than a block, and amendments coloured by hand on the 1944 copy, are not included. The map sheet does not cover the whole 1938 graded area: of the 56 HOLC areas, two (one C, 4.4 km², and one D, 1.2 km²) lie off the sheet, and zoning shares are computed over the land on the sheet only; districts and tracts less than half on the sheet are left missing.

runs.t: S4. Parcel matching, regulatory status and the archival check

text: S4. Parcel matching, regulatory status and the archival check

runs.t: Each geocoded Denver site was matched to the City and County of Denver assessor parcel within 40 m whose situs address matches the directory address, else the parcel on the same street and side with the nearest house number, else the nearest parcel on the same street, else the nearest parcel. All 1,112 manufacturers' sites of 1965–92 and all 267 pre-1960 street-located trades have a parcel within 40 m; the median distance is 4 m, and the situs address matches the directory address outright for 46% of the manufacturers' sites and 23% of the pre-1960 trades. Where several parcels fall within the radius, as for condominium units sharing a footprint, the nearest is taken; the assessor's property class is the same across such units but the dwelling-unit count refers to one of them. Broad classes were assigned from the assessor's class text: residential (single-family, duplex, rowhouse, condominium, apartment, mixed-use residential), industrial and utility (industrial, warehouse, utility, railroad), commercial and office (commercial, office, retail, hotel, parking, service garage), vacant, park and open space (park, golf, cemetery, exempt open space), civic, school and health (exempt school, church, hospital, government, stadium, jail). Regulatory status was assigned from EPA's Facility Registry Service, TRI, SEMS, ACRES brownfields and RCRA (handlers and corrective action) and from Colorado's cleanup, Superfund, brownfield, voluntary-cleanup, UMTRA, solid-waste and environmental-covenant registers, matched by location (40–100 m by inventory, grown by the site's spread up to 250 m), by a record at the same address (street type and unit ignored) or by name; under this rule 1,242 of the 3,487 Colorado sites (36%) match no record. A geocoding error of tens of metres can move a site across those thresholds, so a site with no match is a lead for records review rather than a finding, and absence from the searched inventories is not evidence that a site was never assessed or remediated.

runs.t: For 108 of the 171 residential sites of 1965–92 the present building was built in or before the site's last listing year; 45 were built later and 18 have no date. Most residential sites are therefore small firms in or beside dwellings, or geocodes that fell on a neighbouring dwelling, rather than conversions. Of the 96 residential sites with no record in the searched inventories, 75 are of this kind.

runs.t: An interactive application accompanies the paper. It maps every site, pre-1960 trade, district, tract, HOLC area, 1925 zoning district and matched parcel behind the tables, with the same filters (directory years, sectors, regulatory status, location confidence) applied throughout, and provides the derived data for download: the geocoded listings by edition, the site inventory and firm histories, the district and tract panels, the 1929 zoning districts and their shares by HOLC area and tract, the boundary gaps and change models with their robustness columns, and the parcel matches. Microdata and address files from IPUMS and Brown University are not redistributed.
